problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=4-{t}^{2}$, where $t>0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=0\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.

activity_context.topic_title: Determining Characteristics of Moving Objects Using Integration

feedback.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time  in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=1\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}$ of the particle and determine the earliest time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity.
feedback.worked_solution:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\pi n \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}n,\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is any integer. 

Therefore, the extrema of the velocity function, for $t>0,$ are

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{3\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4},…
$$

We now test the extrema values, starting with the least, using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-12\cdot 1 \\  & =-12<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{4})<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
Therefore, the first time when the particle reaches its maximum velocity is $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int 6\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+C & =1 \\ 0+C & =1\,⟹\,C=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(\frac{\pi }{4})=1+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}.
$$

So the maximum velocity ${v}_{\text{max}}=4\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ is reached first time at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{s}.$
